BEGIN RID PROTOCOL  

STEP 1 — PRE-COMMITMENT  

Causal identification strategy:  
• Use the “shift–share” (Bartik) measure of change in Chinese import exposure per worker for each commuting zone (CZ), 1990-2007.  
• Address endogeneity of U.S. demand shocks with a leave-one-out supply-driven instrument: construct the same shift–share measure but replace U.S. imports with Chinese export growth to eight other high-income countries (Australia, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, Spain, Switzerland).  
• Estimate 2SLS regressions at the CZ level with census-region fixed effects and baseline CZ characteristics as controls. Robust (Eicker-Huber-White) standard errors, clustered by state.  

Directional hypothesis (H): Greater Chinese import exposure lowers manufacturing employment and real wages and raises transfer-payment receipts in U.S. CZs. Formally, βEmp < 0, βWage < 0, βTransfer > 0.  

STEP 2 — SPECIFICATION DISCIPLINE (no more than 5)  

Data set: one CZ-level cross-section with changes computed between 1990 and 2007.  
Controls (identical across specifications):  
  • Baseline (1990) manufacturing employment share,  
  • Baseline (1990) population share with college+,  
  • Baseline (1990) share of foreign-born,  
  • Region fixed effects (Northeast, Midwest, South, West).

Specification 1 (OLS):  
ΔEmpShare_i = α + β_OLS ΔExposure_i + γ′Controls_i + ε_i.

Specification 2 (2SLS for employment):  
First stage: ΔExposure_i = π ΔExposure_IV_i + γ′Controls_i + ν_i.  
Second stage: ΔEmpShare_i = α + β_IV Δ̂Exposure_i + γ′Controls_i + ε_i.

Specification 3 (2SLS for log real wages):  
ΔlogWage_i = α + β_Wage Δ̂Exposure_i + γ′Controls_i + ε_i.

Specification 4 (2SLS for transfers per capita):  
ΔTransfers_i = α + β_Trans Δ̂Exposure_i + γ′Controls_i + ε_i.

Specification 5 (falsification / pre-trend):  
PreΔEmpShare80-90_i = α + φ ΔExposure_IV_i + γ′Controls_i + ε_i.  

No additional specifications will be run.

STEP 3 — FALSIFICATION GATE  

Hypothesis is rejected if ANY of the following hold:  
A. Employment effect β_IV ≥ 0 or two-sided p-value > 0.10.  
B. First-stage F-statistic < 10.  
C. Pre-trend coefficient φ statistically different from zero at 10 % (|t| > 1.64).  
D. Wage effect β_Wage ≥ 0 or p > 0.10.  
E. Transfer effect β_Trans ≤ 0 or p > 0.10.

STEP 4 — R CODE (self-contained)

```r
#------------------------------------------------------------
#  Chinese Import Competition and U.S. Local Labor Markets
#  RID Protocol – Pre-committed Specifications
#------------------------------------------------------------
# Required packages
library(AER)        # for ivreg
library(lmtest)     # for coeftest (robust SE)
library(sandwich)   # for vcovCL cluster-robust
library(readr)      

#------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Load data (one row per commuting zone)
# Expected columns:
#   cz                        Commuting-zone identifier
#   delta_emp_share           Δ manufacturing-employment share 1990-2007
#   delta_exposure            Δ import exposure per worker (U.S. flows)
#   delta_exposure_iv         Instrument (Chinese exports to 8 countries)
#   delta_log_wage            Δ log real average wage 1990-2007
#   delta_transfers_pc        Δ transfers per capita 1990-2007
#   base_manu_share           Baseline 1990 manufacturing-employment share
#   base_college_share        Baseline 1990 college+ share
#   base_foreign_share        Baseline 1990 foreign-born share
#   region                    Factor with 4 census regions
#   pre_delta_emp80_90        Δ manu-emp share 1980-1990
#   state_fips                2-digit state code (for clustering)
#------------------------------------------------------------
df <- read_csv("cz_data.csv")

# Helper: cluster-robust SE at state level
cl_vcov <- function(model){
  vcovCL(model, cluster = df$state_fips)
}

#------------------------------------------------------------
# Specification 1: OLS (employment)
spec1 <- lm(delta_emp_share ~ delta_exposure + 
              base_manu_share + base_college_share + 
              base_foreign_share + factor(region), data = df)
coeftest(spec1, vcov = cl_vcov(spec1))

#------------------------------------------------------------
# Specification 2: 2SLS (employment)
spec2 <- ivreg(delta_emp_share ~ delta_exposure + 
                 base_manu_share + base_college_share + 
                 base_foreign_share + factor(region) |
                 delta_exposure_iv + 
                 base_manu_share + base_college_share + 
                 base_foreign_share + factor(region),
               data = df)
# First-stage F
fsum <- summary(spec2, diagnostics = TRUE)
fs_Fstat <- fsum$diagnostics["Weak instruments","F"]
# Robust SE
coeftest(spec2, vcov = cl_vcov(spec2))

#------------------------------------------------------------
# Specification 3: 2SLS (log real wages)
spec3 <- ivreg(delta_log_wage ~ delta_exposure + 
                 base_manu_share + base_college_share + 
                 base_foreign_share + factor(region) |
                 delta_exposure_iv + 
                 base_manu_share + base_college_share + 
                 base_foreign_share + factor(region),
               data = df)
coeftest(spec3, vcov = cl_vcov(spec3))

#------------------------------------------------------------
# Specification 4: 2SLS (transfers per capita)
spec4 <- ivreg(delta_transfers_pc ~ delta_exposure + 
                 base_manu_share + base_college_share + 
                 base_foreign_share + factor(region) |
                 delta_exposure_iv + 
                 base_manu_share + base_college_share + 
                 base_foreign_share + factor(region),
               data = df)
coeftest(spec4, vcov = cl_vcov(spec4))

#------------------------------------------------------------
# Specification 5: Pre-trend falsification
spec5 <- lm(pre_delta_emp80_90 ~ delta_exposure_iv + 
              base_manu_share + base_college_share + 
              base_foreign_share + factor(region), data = df)
coeftest(spec5, vcov = cl_vcov(spec5))

#------------------------------------------------------------
# Save key statistics for RID gate
out <- list(
  beta_IV = coef(spec2)["delta_exposure"],
  p_IV    = coeftest(spec2, vcov = cl_vcov(spec2))["delta_exposure","Pr(>|t|)"],
  first_stage_F = fs_Fstat[1],
  pretrend_beta = coef(spec5)["delta_exposure_iv"],
  pretrend_p    = coeftest(spec5, vcov = cl_vcov(spec5))["delta_exposure_iv","Pr(>|t|)"],
  beta_Wage = coef(spec3)["delta_exposure"],
  p_Wage   = coeftest(spec3, vcov = cl_vcov(spec3))["delta_exposure","Pr(>|t|)"],
  beta_Trans = coef(spec4)["delta_exposure"],
  p_Trans  = coeftest(spec4, vcov = cl_vcov(spec4))["delta_exposure","Pr(>|t|)"]
)
print(out)
#------------------------------------------------------------
```

STEP 5 — FINDINGS & GATE ASSESSMENT (expected ex-ante)  

Expected numerical signs (approximate magnitudes in parentheses):  
• β_IV (employment) ≈ −0.75 ppt per $1,000 increase in exposure; p ≈ 0.01.  
• First-stage F ≈ 30 ⇒ passes weak-instrument threshold.  
• β_Wage ≈ −0.035 log-points (≈ −3.5 %) per $1,000; p ≈ 0.03.  
• β_Trans ≈ +120 USD per capita; p ≈ 0.04.  
• Pre-trend φ ≈ 0.02 (insignificant; p ≈ 0.55).

Gate assessment: none of the rejection conditions A–E expected to bind. Therefore, on anticipated results, the falsification gate would NOT be triggered, and the directional hypothesis would be retained.

END RID PROTOCOL

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Difference-in-differences with continuous treatment intensity (shift-share / Bartik instrument) — commuting zones with higher initial-year manufacturing industry shares in China-competing sectors are more exposed (continuous treatment); the time variation comes from the decade-specific surge in Chinese imports (1990-2000 and 2000-2007); IV using Chinese exports to other developed countries to address endogeneity

key_variables.treatment: change in Chinese import exposure per worker (continuous, Bartik/shift-share), instrumented by Chinese exports to 8 other developed countries
key_variables.control: commuting zones with low initial exposure to China-competing manufacturing industries
key_variables.outcome: change in manufacturing employment per working-age population; change in average weekly wages; change in transfer receipts per capita (disability, retirement, income assistance)

_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Rising Chinese import competition causes significant declines in manufacturing employment and wages in exposed commuting zones; a $1,000 per worker increase in import exposure reduces manufacturing employment by 0.60 percentage points and increases transfer payments by $58 per capita; effects are concentrated in manufacturing and do not spill over as positive reallocation to other local sectors
_ground_truth.main_effect: A $1,000/worker increase in import exposure reduces manufacturing employment/population by 0.596 percentage points (2SLS); total transfer receipts increase by $58 per capita
key_robustness: First-stage F-statistic > 10 for the shift-share instrument
Controlling for demographic composition, routine-task intensity, offshorability
Removing top import-competing industries one at a time

identification_strategy_detail.treatment: Shift-share measure: Δ import exposure per worker = Σ_j (L_ij0 / L_i0) × (ΔM_UCj / L_j0), weighted by initial industry employment shares
identification_strategy_detail.unit_of_observation: Commuting zone × decade (722 CZs × 2 periods = 1,444 observations)
identification_strategy_detail.key_assumption: Chinese export growth to other developed countries (instrument) captures supply-driven Chinese productivity gains that are exogenous to U.S. local labor demand shocks. Initial industry composition (employment shares) is predetermined and does not reflect anticipated future Chinese competition.

key_magnitudes.manufacturing_employment: -0.596 pp per $1,000/worker increase in import exposure (2SLS, SE=0.134)
key_magnitudes.total_employment: Not significantly offset by non-manufacturing employment gains
key_magnitudes.transfer_payments: +$58 per capita in total transfers ($36 disability + $22 other) per $1,000/worker import exposure
key_magnitudes.wage_effect: Average weekly wage falls by approximately $36 per $1,000/worker import exposure

_ground_truth.robustness_notes_detail: Results are robust to a wide range of controls including initial CZ characteristics, demographic composition, computer adoption, routine-task intensity, and state fixed effects. First-stage F-statistics exceed 20, ruling out weak instrument concerns. Pre-trend analysis (1980-1990) shows no relationship between 1990s import exposure and 1980s employment changes, supporting exogeneity. OLS estimates are smaller than IV, consistent with attenuation bias from measurement error in the trade exposure variable.
